scenario: AITA for apparently being "unable to accept my husband as he is"? | I am married to the most generous, humble, kind hearted, gracious but non-talkative man I know. We have two girls and a boy together and things between us have been great in the past, but there has been an issue between us which we rugswept which I do want to hash out. The issue being, where my husband is very quiet and withdrawn, I am sociable and outgoing. This has led me to struggles in trying to get him involved in a wide range of parties and events, I remember practically begging him to be involved with the dual wedding of my two sisters; where I begged him to at least attend the event and make small talk the guests and the grooms, he did at least attend, but he sat in the corner drinking a beer, brooding over I don't know what. It's always been like that with him, where I encourage him to break out of his shell and make new friends, he tells me he's not big on talking to people he doesn't know too well or like that much. It's gotten to the point that our teenage son has told me that he wants to be closer to his father and taken to all sorts of fun boy stuff such as sports games and concerts. I take our girls out to do girl stuff all the time, and sometimes our son feels compelled to jump in the car with us to escape his father who he deeply loves but has admitted he finds boring. I've questioned my husband if he may want to speak to someone about his isolating tendencies, but he repeatedly tells me he is fine, it's just who he is; as a child he was raised by loudmouths, so he doesn't feel too compelled to act out and that he has a "perfectly extroverted wife" to watch and admire as she deals with people. This simply isn't good enough for me; he's got so few friends and they pretty much all from work and he doesn't have any sort of social media, hobbies or anything. He just likes to be "alone", if alone is with the family or at home. After finishing up dinner and the kids were sleeping, I talked to my older sister about this the other day on the phone . I just vented and she listened. I complained that my husband might have depression. I said that I was worried that he would never have a social life of his own outside of work. I was at this point, getting irritated and said "God, I can't stand that loner sometimes". This was heard by my husband who was upset about this statement. After the phone call, he had an angry tone in his voice and said "why won't you just accept me as I am, Gem? Am I that unlikable to you that you need me out of the house or something? I like being a loner. I like being quiet and introverted. I already have you to balance this out. Why can't you just accept that?" I backed off with making complaints about his loneliness and styed quiet as he scolded me for wanting him to change himself. He's been broody ever since this little argument. My sisters got the gist of it in subsequent phone calls and agreed that I shouldn't have been so forceful in wanting him to change. But AITA for just wanting him to be more social?

First, the wife describes her husband as generous, humble, kind-hearted, and gracious, but also as quiet and withdrawn. She's outgoing and sociable, which has led to some struggles in getting him involved in parties and events. For example, she remembers begging him to attend her sisters' dual wedding, and while he did attend, he sat in the corner drinking beer and brooding. He mentions that as a child, he was raised by loudmouths, so he doesn't feel compelled to act out and that he has a "perfectly extroverted wife" to watch and admire as she deals with people. The wife feels this isn't good enough. Her husband has few friends, mostly from work, and doesn't have any social media, hobbies, or anything else. He just likes to be alone, even if it's with the family or at home. After a phone call with her older sister where she vented about her husband's loneliness and worried he'd never have a social life outside of work, she said, "God, I can't stand that loner sometimes." Her husband overheard this and was upset, asking why she can't accept him as he is. He's been brooding ever since. The wife's sister agreed that she shouldn't have been so forceful in wanting him to change. Now, the wife is wondering if she's AITA (Are You the Asshole?) for just wanting her husband to be more social. So, is it morally acceptable for the wife to want her husband to be more social? Let's consider the factors. On one hand, the wife wants her husband to be more involved in family activities and social events to strengthen their relationship and provide a better environment for their children. She's concerned about her husband's social isolation and its impact on their family life. On the other hand, her husband has clearly expressed that he's content with his introverted nature and doesn't feel the need to change. He's comfortable with his quiet, alone time and doesn't see the value in expanding his social circle beyond work. There's also the aspect of mutual respect in a marriage. The wife wants her husband to change, but he's resistant. She's expressed her concerns to her sister, which led to an argument and hurt feelings. Additionally, the children's feelings are involved. The son feels compelled to join his mother's activities to escape his father, which might indicate a lack of connection between the son and father. So, is it morally acceptable for the wife to push her husband to be more social? Or is she overstepping by trying to change him? I think it's important to consider the balance between personal happiness and the well-being of the family. While the wife has valid concerns about her husband's social isolation and its impact on their family, it's also crucial to respect her husband's autonomy and his right to be who he is. Attempting to change someone against their will can lead to resentment and damage the relationship. It's possible that the wife's persistence in wanting her husband to be more social is coming across as disrespectful or dismissive of his personality and needs. However, it's also important for the wife to express her feelings and concerns in a constructive manner, rather than venting to her sister in a way that her husband could overhear. Communication is key, but it needs to be done with empathy and understanding. In conclusion, while the wife's intentions may be good in wanting to strengthen their family and improve their social life, pushing her husband to change in a way that he's resistant to can be seen as morally unacceptable. It's essential to find a balance between expressing concerns and respecting her husband's right to be himself.
